title: Taser review too late for Roman
article: To say she's "happy" B.C.'s police complaint commissioner has ordered an investigation into the use of Taser guns might be an over statement.
Diana Andreichikov has known little happiness of late.

The Richmond mother is still wracked with anguish about the death of her eldest son, 25-year-old Roman Andreichikov, who died 15 minutes after he had been tasered and put in handcuffs by officers at a downtown Granville Street apartment May 1.
"It's not going to make any difference to me, and my life, or my son's life. But that's good they're investigating," said the grieving mother.

The external investigation, headed by Victoria Police Chief Paul Battershill, is in response to growing concern about the use of Taser guns, which have been linked to four deaths in B.C. in just over a year.
Most recently, Robert Bagnell, 44, stopped breathing shortly after police subdued him with a Taser gun in a bathroom at Vancouver's Continental Hotel where Bagnell was on a rampage.

Bagnell died at the scene early June 23, but Vancouver police neglected to inform Bagnell's family that he had been shot with a Taser until a month later - and then the family only found out through media reports.
The Taser, used by many police forces, including Richmond's, is a stun gun that temporarily incapacitates suspects by emitting up to 50,000 volts through a pair of electrodes.
Police complaint commissioner Dirk Ryneveld has requested the investigation pay special attention to the issue of Taser guns being used on people high on drugs.
Bagnell was HIV-positive and had consumed what police described as "lethal levels" of cocaine, as well as other drugs, before he was tasered.

In the case of Richmond's Andreichikov, Vancouver Police Department spokeswoman Const. Sarah Bloor said officers had been called to the Granville Street apartment by Andreichikov's friend who reported Andreichikov had been on a five-day drug binge and threatened to jump off a fourth-floor balcony.

Also of concern is anyone with a weak heart, said Emile Therien, president of the Canada Safety Council, who pointed to a 1989 study which found that stun guns induced heart attacks in pigs with pacemakers.
"These Taser guns have been in use in Canada since about 1999, 2000, so it's time to have a review."
In fact, he would like to see the investigation go beyond B.C., and be national in scope.

"We're not saying Tasers should be withdrawn. In a lot of cases, they are a lot better than the alternative. But we are calling for a comprehensive, national review into when and how these weapons are used," Therien added.
